text: By the end of the 1800s, physics looked essentially finished. Then three stubborn experimental facts refused to fit, and the fix physicists were forced into is the same fix that makes a qubit behave nothing like a classical bit.

First, hot glowing objects: classical physics says every vibration mode of a hot object's electromagnetic field should get an equal share of thermal energy, and since there are vastly more high-frequency modes than low-frequency ones, that predicts infinite radiated energy at ultraviolet frequencies — the ultraviolet catastrophe. Real objects obviously don't do this. Second, the photoelectric effect: shine dim light below a certain threshold frequency on a metal, and no amount of brightness ever ejects an electron, while even faint light above that threshold ejects electrons immediately. Third, heat a thin gas and look at its light through a prism — you see a handful of sharp lines, not a continuous rainbow, and every element has its own exact, reproducible fingerprint of lines.

Each failure got the same kind of fix. Planck, in 1900, assumed vibrating modes can only exchange energy in discrete chunks tied to frequency — high-frequency modes need chunks too big for ordinary thermal energy to supply, so they stay unexcited and the catastrophe never happens. Einstein, in 1905, explained the photoelectric effect by treating light itself as discrete photons, each one's energy fixed by frequency alone — a below-threshold photon is just too weak, no matter how many arrive per second. And atoms, it turned out, can only sit at specific fixed energy levels, so they only ever emit light at the exact wavelengths matching the gaps between those levels. In every case, energy that classical physics assumed was continuous turned out to come in discrete, countable units.

This matters directly for you as a software engineer learning quantum computing. A classical bit is a direct descendant of classical physics's comfortable assumptions — a voltage engineers deliberately pin to one of two stable, deterministic values. A qubit is built on exactly the physics that broke those assumptions: discrete allowed outcomes and probabilistic behavior, with even position and momentum resisting the kind of definite trajectory classical mechanics assumes, as the next lesson will show directly.

Next lesson: the double-slit experiment, the single most famous demonstration that particles aren't tiny bullets following definite paths — and the key to understanding why quantum algorithms work at all.
